titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Sharing the spoil; Minaya sent to King Alfonso with a gift (tiradas 40–43, lines 778–835b)
part: Tiradas 40–43 · Sharing the spoil; Minaya sent to King Alfonso with a gift (lines 778–835b)

sentences.t:
A Mynaya Álbar Fáñez bien l'anda el cavallo,
daquestos moros mató treinta e quatro;
espada tajador, sangriento trae el braço,
por el cobdo ayuso la sangre destellando.
sentences.l:
To Mynaya Álbar Fáñez well for-him goes the horse,
of-these Moors he-killed thirty and four;
sword cutting, bloody he-brings the arm,
by the elbow downward the blood dripping.
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez's horse carries him well; of these Moors he killed thirty-four; his sword is keen, his arm comes back bloody, the blood running down past the elbow.
sentences.n: Tirada 40 (assonance á-o) — Minaya sees his vow fulfilled; the spoil of the battle; the Çid prepares a present for the king (Pidal: Minaya ve cumplido su voto. — Botín de la batalla. — El Cid dispone un presente para el Rey). Every line ends in á-o (cavallo, quatro, braço, destellando). The scene picks up from vv. 752–756, where the Çid gave Minaya a fresh horse. l'anda = le anda, 'goes for him' (the le cut to l' before the vowel): the horse serves him well. Mynaya, with y, is the print's spelling here, Minaya elsewhere. daquestos = de aquestos, 'of these'. espada tajador, 'his sword cutting', a phrase without a verb; adjectives in -dor have one form for both genders in Old Spanish, so tajador goes with feminine espada. trae, 'brings, has' (traer often just 'to carry about one'). cobdo = codo, 'elbow'; ayuso, 'downward'. destellando, 'dripping' (Latin destillare), the word used of Fáriz's wound in v. 762; the whole line repeats v. 501 of Minaya's vow (e por el cobdo ayuso la sangre destellando), which is here fulfilled to the letter (see v. 782).

sentences.t:
Dize Minaya: “agora so pagado,
que a Castiella irán buenos mandados,
que mio Çid Roy Díaz lid campal a [arrancado].”
sentences.i: Minaya says: “Now I am content, for good tidings will go to Castile, that my Çid Ruy Díaz has won a pitched battle.”
sentences.n: so = soy, 'I am'. pagado, 'satisfied, content' (pagar, 'to please, satisfy'; the money sense is secondary): Pidal notes that in saying agora so pagado Minaya alludes to the vow he made at v. 498, fata que yo me pague … 'until I have satisfied myself …'. mandados, 'tidings, news'. lid campal, 'pitched battle, battle in the open field'. a [arrancado] = ha arrancado, 'has won' (arrancar la lid, 'to win the battle'; compare rancado, v. 764); the h of the auxiliary is not written, and the whole word arrancado is in italics in Pidal's print, i.e. supplied by him. Roy = Ruy. On the scan (checked at 500 dpi) the o of Roy is in italics here, as at v. 828, so Pidal's print reads R[o]y; the pinned text has Roy without the bracket, which is left for the owner to correct.

sentences.t:
Tantos moros yazen muertos que pocos bivos a dexados.
ca en alcaz sin dubda les f[o]ron dando.
sentences.l:
So-many Moors lie dead that few alive he-has left,
for in pursuit without doubt to-them they-went giving.
sentences.i: So many Moors lie dead that few are left alive, for in the pursuit they kept laying into them without fear.
sentences.n: yazen, 'lie' (yazer = yacer). a dexados = ha dexado, 'has left' (dexar = dejar), the participle agreeing in the plural with pocos bivos, as Old Spanish often lets it agree with the object; the subject is left loose — the Çid, named in v. 784, his host, or Minaya, whose feats open the tirada. In Pidal's print the last word, dexados, does not fit on its line and is set at the end of the next after a bracket; here it is put back in its own line. ca, 'for'. en alcaz, 'in the pursuit' (Pidal on v. 772, see the previous part). sin dubda: 'without fear', or 'without doubt, surely': dubda in Old Spanish is both 'doubt' and 'fear' (dubdar, 'to fear'), and the line does not decide between them; the translation takes 'without fear'. les f[o]ron dando = les fueron dando, 'they kept giving it to them' (ir + gerund; colpes, 'blows', understood); the o of f[o]ron is Pidal's. The tenses shift between present and past, as usual.

sentences.t: Yas tornan los del que en buen ora nasco.
sentences.l: Already-themselves turn-back those of-him who in good hour was-born.
sentences.i: Now the men of him who was born in a good hour are turning back.
sentences.n: yas = ya se, 'already themselves': se tornan, 'they turn back' from the chase. los del que en buen ora nasco, 'those of him who was born in a good hour', the Çid's men; nasco, old strong preterite of nacer.

sentences.t:
Andava mio Çid sobre so buen cavallo,
la cofia fronzida ¡Dios, cómmo es bien barbado!
almófar a cuestas, la espada en la mano.
sentences.l:
Was-going my Çid upon his good horse,
the coif gathered — God, how he-is well bearded! —
mail-hood on back, the sword in the hand.
sentences.i: My Çid was riding on his good horse, his coif gathered close — God, how fine a beard he has! — his mail hood thrown back on his shoulders, sword in hand.
sentences.n: Andava, imperfect of andar, 'was going about'. so = su. cofia, the cloth cap worn under the mail hood; fronzida, 'gathered, puckered' (modern fruncida). almófar (Arabic), the hood of mail; a cuestas, 'on the back'. Pidal: the coif gathered about the face (fruncida sobre la cara) and the mail hood fallen onto the shoulders left the Çid's beard fully uncovered; he refers to his introduction (pp. 105–106) and v. 2059. The beard is the Çid's mark of honour, and the minstrel breaks off to admire it: ¡Dios, cómmo es bien barbado!, 'God, how well bearded he is!' (cómmo = cómo; the ¡ is Pidal's).

sentences.t:
Vio los sos commos van allegando:
“Grado a Dios, aquel que está en alto,
quando tal batalla avemos arrancado.”
sentences.l:
He-saw the his-men how-themselves they-go gathering:
“Thanks to God, him who is on high,
when such battle we-have won.”
sentences.i: He saw his men coming in and gathering: “Thanks be to God on high, now that we have won such a battle.”
sentences.n: los sos, 'his men' (sos = sus). commos = commo se, 'how they' (the enclitic squeeze again): se van allegando, 'they come gathering, assembling' (allegarse; ir + gerund). Grado: Pidal, 'agradecimiento', 'thanks', much used in exclamations (vv. 1118, 1267, 2456 etc.), sometimes beside its synonym gracias (vv. 895, 2095). aquel que está en alto, 'him who is on high'; compare v. 8. quando, 'since, now that'. avemos arrancado, 'we have won' (aver as auxiliary; Pidal cites this line for arrancar la batalla in his note on v. 764).

sentences.t:
Esta albergada los de mio Çid luego la an robad[o]
de escudos e de armas e de otros averes largos;
de los moriscos, quando son llegados,
ffallaron quinientos e diez cavallos.
sentences.l:
This camp those of my Çid at-once it they-have plundered
of shields and of arms and of other riches abundant;
of the Moorish-ones, when they-are come,
they-found five-hundred and ten horses.
sentences.i: My Çid's men at once stripped the camp of shields and arms and other plentiful riches; of the Moors' horses, when they came to them, they found five hundred and ten.
sentences.n: albergada: Pidal, the 'campamento', the encampment of the besiegers spoken of at v. 656. Esta albergada … la, the object stated first and taken up again by the pronoun. luego, 'at once' (not modern 'later'). robar X de Y, 'to strip X of Y'; the o of robad[o] is Pidal's. averes largos: Pidal (on v. 804), 'riquezas abundantes', 'abundant wealth' (cf. vv. 481, 1972 etc.); aver here is the noun, 'goods, property'. de los moriscos, 'of the Moorish ones' (horses understood). son llegados, 'they have come' (llegar takes ser). ffallaron = fallaron, 'they found', the double ff a scribal spelling of initial f-, kept as printed (f- for modern h-: hallaron). The line number 796b is Pidal's own.

sentences.t:
Grand alegreya va entre essos cristianos,
más de quinze de los sos menos non fallaron.
sentences.l:
Great joy goes among those Christians,
more than fifteen of the their-own missing not they-found.
sentences.i: Great is the rejoicing among those Christians: they found no more than fifteen of their own missing.
sentences.n: alegreya, 'joy' (an old form of alegría). va, 'goes', i.e. 'there is'. fallar menos: Pidal, 'echar de menos', 'to miss' (cf. v. 1260): non fallaron menos más de quinze, 'they did not miss more than fifteen', so the Christian dead were few. de los sos, 'of their own'.

sentences.i: They carry away gold and silver past all reckoning; all those Christians are made rich again by the gain they had found there.
sentences.n: que non saben recabdo, 'that they know no reckoning of it', so much they cannot count it (recabdo, 'account, tally'). refechos, 'remade', i.e. replenished, made wealthy again (refazer, f- for modern h-). aquesta = esta. y, 'there'. avién, 'had' (imperfect of aver, = habían). The second half of v. 800b, que y avién fallado, is printed in italics by Pidal: it is his restoration. The number 800b is his own.

sentences.t:
A so castiello a los moros dentro los an tornados,
mandó mio Çid aun que les diessen algo.
sentences.l:
To their castle to the Moors inside them they-have turned-back,
ordered my Çid even that to-them they-should-give something.
sentences.i: They have let the Moors back into their castle, and my Çid ordered that they should even be given something.
sentences.n: Pidal: before the battle the Moorish inhabitants of the castle had been put outside, as v. 679 tells; now they are let back in. so, 'their' (su). a los moros … los, the object marked by a and taken up again by los; tornados agrees with it. aun, 'even, besides'. diessen, imperfect subjunctive of dar. The Çid's generosity to the conquered townsfolk is a theme of the poem.

sentences.i: Great is the joy my Çid has with all his vassals. He had this money and these plentiful riches shared out; in his fifth a hundred horses fall to the Çid.
sentences.n: Grant a el gozo, 'great joy has' (a = ha, from aver 'to have'). Dio a partir, 'he gave to be divided', i.e. had the spoil shared out. dineros, 'money, coin'. averes largos, 'abundant riches', as v. 795. la su quinta, article + possessive: the lord's fifth, the share of booty due to the leader. Pidal on v. 805: 'remember v. 796b' — a hundred of the five hundred and ten horses, roughly a fifth. caen, 'fall (to him)'.

sentences.t:
¡Dios, qué bien pagó a todos sus vassallos,
a los peones e a los encavalgados!
sentences.l:
God, how well he-paid all his vassals,
the foot-soldiers and the mounted-men!
sentences.i: God, how well he rewarded all his vassals, the men on foot and the horsemen alike!
sentences.n: pagó, 'paid', and also 'satisfied' — pagar has both senses here (see v. 782). sus, here with u, beside sos in v. 803; the text keeps both. peones, 'foot-soldiers'; encavalgados, 'mounted men'. The ¡ and ! are Pidal's.

sentences.t:
Bien lo aguisa el que en buen ora nasco,
quantos él trae todos son pagados.
sentences.l:
Well it arranges he who in good hour was-born,
as-many-as he brings all are satisfied.
sentences.i: He who was born in a good hour arranges it well: all the men he brings with him are content.
sentences.n: aguisar, 'to arrange, dispose' (guisa, 'manner'). el que en buen ora nasco: the formula. quantos él trae todos, 'as many as he brings, all' (trae, 'leads, has with him'). son pagados, 'are satisfied'.

sentences.t:
“Oíd, Minaya, sodes mio diestro braço!
D'aquesta riqueza que el Criador nos a dado
a vuestra guisa prended con vuestra mano.
sentences.l:
“Hear, Minaya, you-are my right arm!
Of-this wealth that the Creator to-us has given
at your liking take with your hand.
sentences.i: “Listen, Minaya, you are my right arm! Of this wealth the Creator has given us, take with your own hand as much as you please.
sentences.n: The Çid speaks; he is not named. Oíd, imperative of oír, 'hear' (the accent is faint on the scan); Pidal prints the exclamation with only the closing !, no opening ¡ (compare v. 706), and the text keeps it so. sodes = sois. mio diestro braço, 'my right arm', as at v. 753. D'aquesta = de aquesta, 'of this' (= de esta). a = ha, 'has'. a vuestra guisa, 'at your will, as you please'. prended, imperative of prender, 'take'.

sentences.t:
Enbiar vos quiero a Castiella con mandado
desta batalla que avemos arrancad[o];
sentences.l:
To-send you I-want to Castiella with message
of-this battle that we-have won;
sentences.i: I want to send you to Castile with news of this battle we have won;
sentences.n: Enbiar vos quiero, 'I want to send you' (the infinitive placed first, the pronoun after it). mandado, 'message, tidings'. desta = de esta. avemos arrancad[o], 'we have won' (the o is Pidal's).

sentences.t:
al rey Alfons que me a ayrado
quiérol enbiar en don treinta cavallos,
todos con siellas e muy bien enfrenados,
señas espadas de los arzones colga[ndo].”
sentences.l:
to-the king Alfons who me has angered-at
I-want-to-him to-send in gift thirty horses,
all with saddles and very well bridled,
each-one swords from the saddle-bows hanging.”
sentences.i: to King Alfonso, who has turned his anger against me, I want to send thirty horses as a gift, all saddled and finely bridled, each with a sword hanging from the saddle-bow.”
sentences.n: me a ayrado, 'has turned his anger on me' (airar, the king's formal disfavour that sent the Çid into exile). quiérol = quiero + le, 'I want to … him' (the enclitic squeeze; the le doubles al rey Alfons). en don, 'as a gift'. siellas = sillas, 'saddles'; enfrenados, 'bridled'. señas: Pidal, 'sendas' (one to each horse). arzones, 'saddle-bows'. colga[ndo]: the ending is Pidal's. Pidal on v. 816 refers to his introduction (p. 99) on the fifth of captured horses that the Çid sends to the king, and cites a later parallel: after the battle of the Salado in 1340, Alfonso XI of Castile sent to the pope at Avignon horses taken from the Moors, 'e iban ensillados, e cada cavallo llevava una espada e una adarga en el arzón de la silla' ('and they went saddled, and each horse carried a sword and a shield on the saddle-bow'). The vassal in disgrace courts the king who exiled him.

sentences.t: Dixo Minaya Álbar Fáñez: “esto faré yo de grado.”
sentences.l: Said Minaya Álbar Fáñez: “this will-do I with pleasure.”
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez said: “That I will gladly do.”
sentences.n: faré = haré, 'I will do' (fazer, f- for h-). de grado, 'willingly, gladly' (grado, as in v. 792, from Latin gratum).

sentences.i: “Here is gold and fine silver, a boot full to the brim; at Santa María of Burgos have a thousand masses paid for;
sentences.n: Tirada 41 (assonance í-a) — the Çid fulfils his promise to the cathedral of Burgos (Pidal: El Cid cumple su oferta a la catedral de Burgos). The line-ends go to í-a (fina, mingua, missas, fijas, días, ricas). Pidal opens the tirada with a dash: the Çid takes up the word again after Minaya's answer. Evades: Pidal, 'he aquí', 'here is, behold' (cf. v. 253). [fina], 'fine, pure', is supplied by Pidal (printed in italics). uesa lleña: Pidal finds it curious to see the uesa, the high boot (huesa), used as a sack; even when worn, he notes, the boot served for keeping small things in, when clothes had no pockets. lleña, 'full' (llena), is printed so, with ñ; the sense is not in doubt, the spelling is kept as Pidal prints it. que nada nol mingua, 'that nothing is lacking to it', i.e. filled to the top: double negative (nada … non), with nol = non le; mingua = mengua. quitedes: Pidal, 'paguéis', 'pay for' (subjunctive as a command); in this the Çid keeps the promise he made at v. 225. Santa María de Burgos, the cathedral.

sentences.i: whatever is left over, give it to my wife and my daughters, that they may pray for me night and day; if I live, for their sake, they will be wealthy ladies.”
sentences.n: romaneçiere, future subjunctive of romaneçer: Pidal, romanecer and remanecer, 'quedar, sobrar', 'to remain, be left over'. daldo = dadlo, 'give it' (imperative dad + lo, with d and l swapped, as valelde in v. 714). mugier = mujer, 'wife'; fijas = hijas (f- for h-). rueguen, present subjunctive of rogar. las noches e los días, 'night and day'. visquier[o]: Pidal, 'viviere', 'should live', future subjunctive formed on the old perfect visco, 'he lived'; the first person ends in -o (compare fallaro, v. 1260, where the assonance guarantees it), and the final o here is Pidal's. si les yo visquiero, 'if I live for them' (les, for their benefit). dueñas, 'ladies' (Latin domina).

sentences.t:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez desto es pagado;
por ir con él omnes son contados.
sentences.l:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez of-this is satisfied;
for to-go with him men are counted.
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez is content with this; men are counted off to go with him.
sentences.n: Tirada 42 (assonance á-o) — Minaya sets out for Castile (Pidal: Minaya parte para Castilla). The assonance returns to á-o (pagado, contados, entrado, acordando), but Pidal sets the four lines apart as a tirada of their own. desto = de esto. es pagado, 'is content', as v. 782. omnes = hombres. son contados, 'are counted', i.e. picked out by number for the escort. The number 826b is Pidal's own.

sentences.t:
Agora davan çevada, ya la noch [avie] entrad[o],
mio Çid R[o]y Díaz con los sos se acorda[ndo]:
sentences.l:
Now they-were-giving barley, already the night [had] come-in,
my Çid Roy Díaz with the his-men himself consulting:
sentences.i: Now they were feeding barley to the horses — night had already fallen — my Çid Ruy Díaz taking counsel with his men:
sentences.n: davan çevada, 'they were giving barley' — the horses fed at nightfall, ready for an early start. Pidal, in his note on v. 836 ('por la mañana se fué Minaya', 'in the morning Minaya went off'), refers back to this line: the departure follows next morning. noch = noche, cut. [avie] entrad[o], 'had come in': the word avie and the final o are Pidal's. R[o]y = Ruy, only the o in italics here (as at v. 784, where the pinned text lacks the bracket). se acorda[ndo], 'taking counsel' (compare tornós a acordar, v. 666), a gerund with no main verb; the -ndo is Pidal's. The colon leads into the Çid's farewell, which opens the next tirada.

sentences.t:
“¿Ides vos, Minaya, a Castiella la gentil?
A nuestros amigos bien les pode[d]es dezir:
Dios nos valió e vençiemos la lid.
sentences.l:
“Go you, Minaya, to Castiella the noble?
To our friends well to-them you-can say:
God us helped and we-won the battle.
sentences.i: “Are you going, Minaya, to noble Castile? You may well tell our friends: God helped us, and we won the battle.
sentences.n: Tirada 43 (assonance í) — the farewell (Pidal: Despedida). Every line now ends in stressed í (gentil, dezir, lid, aquí). Ides = vais, 'you go': Pidal, for the question used in a leave-taking, compare v. 204. Castiella la gentil, 'noble Castile', as v. 672. les podedes dezir, 'you can tell them' (A nuestros amigos … les, the redundant dative); podedes = podéis, the old -edes ending. pode[d]es: the second d is in italics on the scan (checked at 500 dpi): Pidal's restoration. valió, 'helped' (valer, 'to protect'). vençiemos, an old preterite form, = vencimos. lid, 'battle'.

sentences.t:
A la tornada, si nos falláredes aquí;
si non, do sopiéredes que somos, indos conseguir.
sentences.l:
At the return, if us you-should-find here;
if not, where you-should-know that we-are, go-us to-overtake.
sentences.i: When you come back, if you find us here — well; if not, wherever you learn we are, go on and catch us up.
sentences.n: A la tornada, 'on the return'. falláredes, sopiéredes, future subjunctives of fallar ('find', f- for h-) and saber, normal after si and do in Old Spanish. Pidal glosses the first line 'si nos hallareis aquí, bien; si no …', 'if you find us here, good; if not …' (cf. v. 181): the apodosis is left unsaid. do = donde. indos = idnos, 'go … us' (imperative id + nos, with d and n swapped, as daldo for dadlo in v. 823); the nos is the object of conseguir, set beside the imperative: 'go and overtake us'. conseguir, 'to follow and overtake' (Latin consequi). The Çid expects not to be here long; see v. 835b.

sentences.t:
Por lanças e por espadas avemos de guarir,
si non, en esta tierra angosta non podriemos bivir,
e commo yo cuedo, a ir nos avremos d' aquí.”
sentences.i: By lance and by sword we must win our keep; otherwise we could not live in this poor, narrow land; and, as I reckon, we shall have to move on from here.”
sentences.n: avemos de guarir, 'we have to save ourselves, get our living' (aver de + infinitive, 'to have to'; guarir, 'to be saved, survive'). si non, 'otherwise'. angosta, 'narrow' and so 'poor, scanty' — the barren country round Alcocer (cf. v. 838). podriemos, conditional of poder, 'we could'; bivir = vivir. cuedo, 'I think' (cuedar/cuidar). a ir nos avremos, 'we shall have to go away' (aver a + infinitive; nos belongs with ir, irnos 'to go away', and stands between ir and the future avremos). d' aquí is printed with a space after the apostrophe. The whole of the last line (835b) is printed in italics by Pidal: it is his restoration, not the manuscript's, and is printed here in plain type; it has no number of its own in his margin, and the letter b is a provisional number of ours.
